```{r setup, include = FALSE}
options(digits = 4)

has_recipes <- requireNamespace("recipes", quietly = TRUE)
has_tune <- all(vapply(
  c("recipes", "rsample", "parsnip", "tune", "dials", "workflows",
    "yardstick", "glmnet"),
  requireNamespace, logical(1), quietly = TRUE))
knitr::opts_chunk$set(eval = has_recipes)
```

```{r eval = !has_recipes, echo = FALSE, comment = NA}
cat("The recipes package is not installed, so this vignette's code was not run.\n")
```

Carryover decay, saturation shape and a model's own penalty are not
independent. A longer carryover smooths the media series and lowers its peaks,
which changes which penalty is optimal, which changes which saturation point
best fits the residual curvature. Choosing them one at a time (decay by
cross-validation, saturation by eye, penalty by `glmnet`'s own path) finds a
corner of the parameter space and calls it an optimum.

Tuning them jointly is what the recipe steps `step_adstock()` and
`step_saturation()` are for. It is the entire reason these transforms are
recipe steps rather than functions you call beforehand.

The examples use `mm_weekly`, a simulated weekly panel of media spend and
revenue by geography:

```{r message = FALSE}
library(mediamix)
library(recipes)
data(mm_weekly)

channels <- c("tv", "video", "search", "social", "display")
```

## The problem `step_adstock()` solves

Adstock is a filter with memory. Prepare a recipe on the first two and a half
years and bake it on the rest, and the first rows of the new data have no
history.

A lag built with `recipes::step_lag()` leaves `NA`, or the filler given as its
`default`, in the first rows of new data at every prep/bake boundary, and
dropping those rows with `step_naomit(skip = FALSE)` removes the boundary weeks
from training and evaluation. `step_adstock()` carries the filter's state
across the boundary instead:

```{r}
train <- mm_weekly[mm_weekly$date < as.Date("2025-07-01"), ]
test <- mm_weekly[mm_weekly$date >= as.Date("2025-07-01"), ]

rec <- recipe(revenue ~ ., data = train) |>
  step_adstock(all_of(channels), index = "date", by = "geo", decay = 0.7) |>
  prep()

tidy(rec, number = 1)
```

The `state` column is the filter's memory at the end of training for each
channel and geography. Geometric adstock is the recursion
$a_t = x_t + \theta a_{t-1}$, with $\theta$ the `decay`, so that memory is one
number per series: the last $a_t$, reported before the `normalise` scaling by
$1 - \theta$. `prep()` also keeps each geography's training time points and
media values, so that new data repeating the last periods of training is
filtered exactly too. For this training set they take up
`r format(object.size(rec$steps[[1]]$history), units = "kB", standard = "SI")`,
and they are media only, never the outcome.

Baking new data that continues the training series warm-starts the filter from
that state:

```{r}
baked <- bake(rec, new_data = test)
c(rows_in = nrow(test), rows_out = nrow(baked),
  missing = sum(is.na(baked$tv)))
```

Every row comes back, in its original order, with no missing values at the
boundary, and the values are exactly what filtering the whole series at once
gives:

```{r}
full <- mm_weekly[order(mm_weekly$geo, mm_weekly$date), ]
full$expected <- ave(full$tv, full$geo,
                     FUN = function(z) adstock_geometric(z, decay = 0.7))

check <- merge(baked[, c("date", "geo", "tv")],
               full[, c("date", "geo", "expected")],
               by = c("date", "geo"))
all.equal(check$tv, check$expected)
```

That equality is the step's whole contract, and it is enforced by the test
suite.

## What happens when the data does not continue

`bake()` compares the start of the new data with the training time points
`prep()` stored, and handles each case explicitly. New data that repeats
training weeks continues from the weeks before them:

```{r}
# Repeating the last four training weeks, as rsample::rolling_origin(lag = 4)
# assessment sets do: the repeated rows continue from the weeks before them.
overlap <- mm_weekly[mm_weekly$date > max(train$date) - 4 * 7, ]
baked_overlap <- bake(rec, new_data = overlap)
check_overlap <- merge(baked_overlap[, c("date", "geo", "tv")],
                       full[, c("date", "geo", "expected")],
                       by = c("date", "geo"))
all.equal(check_overlap$tv, check_overlap$expected)

# Repeating the whole training period has nothing before it, so re-baking the
# training data reproduces the prepared output.
all.equal(bake(rec, new_data = train)$tv, juice(rec)$tv)
```

New data that starts after a gap cannot continue the filter, so it
cold-starts with a warning that names the gap:

```{r}
# A gap: cold start, and say so.
gapped <- test[test$date >= as.Date("2025-10-01"), ]
invisible(tryCatch(bake(rec, new_data = gapped),
                   warning = function(w) message(conditionMessage(w))))
```

New data that starts less than one period after a training week, as when daily
rows are baked into a weekly step or the reporting day moves, is misaligned;
it cold-starts and warns the same way, as does an unseen group. That is the
default, `carry_over = "auto"`. `carry_over = "warm"` turns those warnings
into errors when you want the pipeline to insist on contiguity;
`carry_over = "cold"` disables state entirely, so each bake filters the new
data on its own, as a lag-based step does.

The step is strictly causal, unlike `recipes::step_window()` and
`recipes::step_impute_roll()`, which are centred and fill a series' leading
edge using future values. Used on media, they would leak future spend into
past adstock and inflate in-sample fit. The step also sorts by `index`
internally and restores the original row order before returning, so nothing
downstream ever sees a reordered table.

## Grouping is an argument, not an inherited state

`recipes` steps have no built-in notion of groups, and a `grouped_df` may not
survive into `bake()`. So `step_adstock()` takes the grouping columns
explicitly, in `by`:

```{r}
setequal(train$geo, as.character(baked$geo))
tidy(rec, number = 1)$group
```

Each geography carries its own state and its own last-seen index. (`prep()`
converts the character `geo` column to a factor along the way, so compare the
values rather than the vectors.)

## Saturation on a comparable scale

Television spend runs to thousands a week here and display to hundreds. An
absolute half-saturation point is therefore a different parameter for every
channel, which makes a single tunable parameter meaningless.

`step_saturation()` expresses it as a *fraction* of each column's own reference
level, learned from the training data:

```{r}
rec2 <- recipe(revenue ~ ., data = train) |>
  step_adstock(all_of(channels), index = "date", by = "geo", decay = 0.7) |>
  step_saturation(all_of(channels), half_max = 0.4, shape = 1.5) |>
  prep()

tidy(rec2, number = 2)
```

`half_max = 0.4` reads the same way for every channel: half the ceiling is
reached at 40% of the largest adstocked value in that channel's training data
(the `reference` column, under the default `ref = "max"`), pooled over the
geographies unless `step_saturation()` is given `by`. One parameter now covers
all five.

## The tuning parameters

Each step tells `tune` which of its arguments can be searched, and mediamix
supplies a `dials` parameter with a default range for each:
`carryover_decay()` and `carryover_max_lag()` for `step_adstock()`, and
`saturation_half_max()` and `saturation_shape()` for `step_saturation()`.

```{r}
carryover_decay()
saturation_shape()
```

```{r}
tunable(rec2$steps[[1]])[, c("name", "source", "component")]
tunable(rec2$steps[[2]])[, c("name", "source", "component")]
```

`carryover_decay()` stops at 0.95 rather than 1 on purpose. A decay of 0.99
implies a half-life of `r round(half_life(0.99))` periods, which no ordinary
media dataset identifies; leaving it in the range mostly spends tuning
iterations on values that trade off against the intercept.

## Joint tuning

One search covers carryover, saturation and the model's penalty together,
scored on rolling-origin resampling of the north geography:

```{r eval = has_tune}
library(rsample)
library(parsnip)
library(workflows)
library(tune)
library(dials)

north <- mm_weekly[mm_weekly$geo == "north", ]
north <- north[order(north$date), ]

folds <- rolling_origin(north, initial = 104, assess = 13, skip = 12,
                        cumulative = TRUE)

tune_rec <- recipe(revenue ~ ., data = north) |>
  # `date` is the filter's index, not a predictor; `geo` is constant within
  # this subset. A recipe does not create dummies by itself, so a leftover
  # character column would reach glmnet's matrix interface and abort.
  update_role(date, new_role = "index") |>
  step_rm(geo) |>
  step_adstock(all_of(channels), index = "date", decay = tune()) |>
  step_saturation(all_of(channels), half_max = tune(), shape = tune()) |>
  step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors())

model <- linear_reg(penalty = tune(), mixture = 0) |>
  set_engine("glmnet")

wf <- workflow() |> add_recipe(tune_rec) |> add_model(model)

params <- extract_parameter_set_dials(wf)
params

# Kept deliberately small so the vignette rebuilds quickly on every check.
# A real search would use more of both.
set.seed(1)
res <- tune_bayes(wf, resamples = folds, param_info = params,
                  initial = 5, iter = 5,
                  metrics = yardstick::metric_set(yardstick::rmse))

show_best(res, metric = "rmse", n = 5)
```

```{r eval = !has_tune, echo = FALSE, comment = NA}
cat("The full tidymodels stack (rsample, parsnip, workflows, tune, dials,\n",
    "yardstick, glmnet) is not installed here, so the chunks that need it\n",
    "were not run. They run in the package's continuous integration, where\n",
    "those packages are installed.\n", sep = "")
```

`show_best()` lists the five best candidates, each a combination of `decay`,
`half_max`, `shape` and `penalty` with its RMSE averaged over the assessment
sets. All four come out of one search, with one resampling scheme and correct
train/test boundaries throughout. Robyn does the equivalent search with the
Python library Nevergrad, so it needs a Python runtime as well as R;
`robyn_mmm()` stops with an error when Nevergrad is not installed.

## One carryover per channel

`tune_rec` applies one `decay` to every column its `step_adstock()` selects,
so the search above tunes a single shared value, which keeps the example
short. Channels rarely share a carryover: in `mm_weekly` the true decays,
stored in `attr(mm_weekly, "truth")`, run from
`r attr(mm_weekly, "truth")$decay[["search"]]` for search to
`r attr(mm_weekly, "truth")$decay[["tv"]]` for television, so for a real
model give each channel its own step. `tune()` takes an identifier, which
keeps the five decays apart in the search:

```{r eval = has_tune}
per_channel <- recipe(revenue ~ ., data = north) |>
  update_role(date, new_role = "index") |>
  step_rm(geo)
for (ch in channels) {
  # `!!` puts the channel name into the step now. A bare `all_of(ch)` is
  # evaluated at prep(), after the loop has finished, so every step would
  # select the last channel.
  per_channel <- step_adstock(per_channel, all_of(!!ch), index = "date",
                              decay = tune(paste0("decay_", ch)))
}
per_channel <- per_channel |>
  step_saturation(all_of(channels), half_max = tune(), shape = tune()) |>
  step_normalize(all_numeric_predictors())

adstock_steps <- Filter(function(s) inherits(s, "step_adstock"),
                        per_channel$steps)
data.frame(
  selects = vapply(adstock_steps,
                   function(s) rlang::quo_text(s$terms[[1]]), character(1)),
  decay = vapply(adstock_steps,
                 function(s) as.character(s$decay[[2]]), character(1))
)
```

Each `step_adstock()` selects one channel and carries its own identifier. The
rest of the recipe is `tune_rec`'s, so `update_recipe(wf, per_channel)` swaps
it into the workflow and the search covers five decays instead of one; give
`tune_bayes()` a larger `initial` and `iter` to match.

## Leakage, since a reviewer will ask

Under rolling-origin resampling, `prep()` re-runs on each split's analysis set.
The stored state is therefore re-learned from that split's training rows alone
and describes only media that precedes the assessment set. Nothing carries
across splits, and no outcome information crosses any boundary: the state is a
function of past *spend*, which is genuinely known at prediction time.

The same argument covers `step_saturation()`: each column's reference level is
a training-set statistic, re-learned per split, and a test-set value above it
is not clipped but lands further up the curve.

## If you skip the tuning, skip the step

The recipe steps add machinery: state, a contiguity guard, a boundary contract
to reason about. All of that earns its place because it makes joint tuning
possible. If you are going to fix decay and saturation by hand anyway, use
`media_transform()` on the vectors and keep your pipeline simpler.
